confirmed: Read the complete local markdown, including the references through its end, and checked decisive passages and every recorded numerical result directly in the PDF. It is the 13-page journal article published 20 May 2025 in International Journal of Innovative Research and Scientific Studies 8(3), printed pp. 3284-3296; the form title and four author names match. Source version is supported (PDF p. 1, title, byline and publication history; PDF p. 13, final reference).

One randomized people study is present: undergraduate English majors in a Communication Skills course at NUML, Islamabad, were randomly divided between no-AI and ChatGPT-3 conditions for a collaborative cardboard-box AUT. Purposive recruitment does not contradict random assignment. field_rct and context_class = none are appropriate (PDF p. 4, printed p. 3287, sections 3.1-3.2.2).

The assignment count is 50 people, 25 per arm, and the reported analyzed count is also 25 per arm, totaling 50 people; this is not a fewer-than-50 experiment. No exclusions are reported. These counts describe students, not ideas, ratings or reflective texts (PDF p. 4, printed p. 3287, section 3.1; PDF p. 5, printed p. 3288, section 4.1).

The model is named ChatGPT-3, without a more precise model identifier. Students received training and queried the tool during the AUT; the task involved a cardboard box and 10 minutes of collaborative idea generation (PDF p. 4, printed p. 3287, sections 3.2.1-3.2.2).

The produced ideas were independently scored by two trained raters for fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration. Flexibility counts categories within the generated ideas; no scored across-people similarity or diversity outcome is reported. Reflection themes about fixation are qualitative perceptions (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 3287-3288, section 3.2.2.3; PDF pp. 6-8, printed pp. 3289-3291, sections 4.6-4.9).

S1-O1 originality and the one-line finding match the PDF: with AI 7.9 ± 2.4 versus without AI 6.1 ± 1.8, n = 25 per arm, t(48) = -3.20, p = .002 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 3288, section 4.1 and Table 1; PDF p. 6, printed p. 3289, section 4.4).
S1-O2 fluency matches the PDF: with AI 22.8 ± 5.3 versus without AI 15.2 ± 4.1, n = 25 per arm, t(48) = -5.80, p < .001 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 3288, sections 4.1-4.2 and Table 1).

S1-O3 flexibility matches the PDF: with AI 11.6 ± 3.1 versus without AI 8.4 ± 2.2, n = 25 per arm, t(48) = -4.27, p < .001 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 3288, section 4.1 and Table 1; PDF p. 6, printed p. 3289, section 4.3).

The form correctly flags the unresolved analysis unit: section 3.2.1 says each group of 25 students generated ideas collaboratively, while section 4.1 and Table 1 report n = 25 per arm and t(48). The paper does not explain conversion of shared output to individual scores or establish independent participant observations (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 3287-3288).

This is an original mixed-methods experiment, not a synthesis; no pooled estimates or synthesis study counts apply. No appendix, supplementary material, preregistration, shared sample, or data/code URL is identified in the complete document (PDF pp. 1-13; methods on pp. 4-5 and references ending on p. 13).

No company involvement is disclosed: the article states no specific financial support and no competing interests. OpenAI is identified as the tool developer (PDF p. 1, Funding and Competing Interests; PDF p. 4, printed p. 3287, section 3.2.2).
summary: The paper reports a classroom randomized study with 50 students analyzed, and the recorded statistics and one-line finding match the PDF. Corrections concern omitted elaboration, incomplete outcome coding, and core eligibility under the supplied rules; the uncertainty about scoring collaborative output still requires review.
